title: Expected value as the balance point of a spinner
examples: How do you work out the expected value of a spinner?

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

explain.say: At a school fair in Mexico there is a spinner with 5 equal parts. Three parts say 1 point and two parts say 6 points. On average, how many points do you win per spin? Look at the left side of the seesaw: the 1 point, with a weight of 3 parts.

draw.text: Expected value as the balance point of a spinner

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

explain.say: Now the right side: the 6 points, with a weight of 2 parts. The weights show how likely each prize is. Where should the pivot go so the seesaw balances? Have a guess.

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

explain.say: At 3 points! The 1 is 2 away from 3, and the 6 is 3 away. Left side: weight 3 times distance 2 is 6. Right side: weight 2 times distance 3 is 6. Equal, so it balances. Look at the left side again.

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

explain.say: Check with sums: 3 spins of 1 plus 2 spins of 6 is 15 points in 5 spins, an average of 3. That balance point is the expected value: what you win per spin in the long run. It is not a prize you can even land on!

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

explain.say: Well done! If one spin costs 3 points, the game is fair. If it costs 4, the stall wins over time. Insurance companies, game designers and casinos all set prices using expected value.

right.label: 6 points: 2 parts
right.ask: Why does the expected value balance?

faq.a: It is the long-run average result of a random game. Multiply each outcome by its probability and add. For this spinner: 3 fifths times 1 plus 2 fifths times 6 equals 3.

faq.q: Why does the expected value balance?
faq.a: Put each outcome on a seesaw as a weight equal to its probability. The point where it balances is the mean, because the pulls on both sides, weight times distance, cancel out.
asks: Why is the mean a balance point?

faq.q: How do you work out the expected value of a spinner?
faq.a: For each prize, multiply its value by the chance of landing on it, then add the results.
asks: How do I calculate expected value?

faq.a: A game is fair when the cost to play equals the expected value of the winnings, so in the long run nobody gains or loses.
asks: What is a fair game in probability?

faq.q: Can the expected value be a result you never get?
faq.a: Yes. This spinner never shows 3, yet 3 is the expected value. A fair die has expected value 3.5, which you can never roll.
asks: Why is expected value 3.5 for a die?

facts: The expected value of a discrete random variable is the sum of each value times its probability.
The expected score on one roll of a fair six-sided die is 3.5.

quiz.say: A spinner has 4 equal parts: 2, 2, 2 and 10 points. What is the expected value?
quiz.show: A spinner has 4 equal parts: 2, 2, 2 and 10 points. What is the expected value?

wrong.0: 2 is the most likely result, but the 10 pulls the average up.
wrong.2: 5 averages 2 and 10 without weighting by how likely they are.

quiz.say: A game costs 5 coins to play and its expected winnings are 3 coins. What happens over many games?
quiz.show: A game costs 5 coins to play and its expected winnings are 3 coins. What happens over many games?

options.show: You win about 2 coins per game
options.say: You win about 2 coins per game

options.show: You lose about 2 coins per game
options.say: You lose about 2 coins per game

wrong.0: The cost is more than the expected winnings, so you lose.
wrong.1: Breaking even needs the cost to equal the expected winnings.
